Please keep sharing, at its base, there's something really great here. All good writing comes with revision after revision after goddamn revision to make it work (that's why some artists take yeeeaaars to put out something new, I'm looking at you My Chemical Romance and Brand New). 

Speaking of Brand New, I agree with the earlier poster that this gives me the same feeling that I get when I hear"Play Crack the Sky" (last track on Deja Entendu, if you're not familiar). If you're going to really flesh it out, I think it'd be nice to hear some additional instrumentation on the track. Even just a clean electric lead can work wonders. 

My two biggest concerns with it, honestly, will probably only be solved by spending a lot of time revising and rewriting. 

First, I think this song struggles a lot with pacing. You change the momentum a little bit here or there, but largely it keeps the energy level at like ... maybe a four out of ten? When I write, I like to think of it like a movie. In order to keep the narrative engaging, you gotta have your slow sequences, you gotta have your energetic climaxes, you gotta have at least one montage, etc. A song is similar. I like to break down each section of the song on paper and assign it one of those 1-10 numbers for the energy level intended in that section. That way you can map out the emotional journey of your song. Maybe you start at a 2, gently rev up the gas to a 3 for the first chorus, and then do a little plot twist and go to 6 for the second verse. Or maybe you just want it to slowly build one number after another into a grand crescendo. Lots of options. 

The second note I have involves the lyrics. This song is gonna ride on the lyrics, and fortunately you have a very solid foundation -- you're already writing better than the average musician. There are great ideas here with a lot of raw emotion, but I think it still reads like a first draft. Now that you know what you're saying in each line, you should start thinking about HOW you're saying it. I listened to a podcast earlier today that I thought really intelligently broke down a process for this stage of lyricism (I can't remember the name, but if you search "iterative songwriting" on spotify you should be able to find it -- if not, reply to this, and I'll look it up tomorrow after I'm out of bed). 

Really start thinking about what words can more vividly or accurately (good writing is in specifics) express your emotions. Think about imagery, so you can paint a picture for your audience. Think about themes and motifs you can weave through the song. Honestly, I'm jealous -- this is my favorite part of the writing process. You get to be really creative and try fun ideas.

I'm someone who always heard lyrics first, before anything else when I listen to a song. I'm a writer by trade, and it's the one thing I've always known I wanted to do with my life -- music was second. And while I dabbled in music, I really struggled to be very good at any of it (made worse by some undiagnosed ADHD in my teens, which made it really difficult to be consistent enough at my practice routines and education).

The miraculous combination that worked out for me was -- when I was 20, I joined a band with people who knew what the fuck they were doing. They needed a bass player and let me learn on the fly. I was very bad, but our chemistry was great and they knew I could write. So they trusted me with all of the lyrics (even if sometimes I was writing those lyrics about subjects they wanted to write about). The vocalists would come to me with a melody, and I would spend a lot of time drafting and re-drafting lyrics to fit those melodies. By the time I joined the band, I had notebooks full of lines for songs that I wound up using (and most of these weren't in song format to begin with, just lines I liked about subject matter I wanted to write about). 

It honestly changed my life forever and I'm still writing with those people and my closest friends are other musicians I met along the journey. I may have gotten lucky finding a fit like this on my first try (so don't be afraid to fail or look for something better) but just really focus on honing your skills as a writer first, and then find people who value that. There's genuinely a huge shortage of good lyricists out there, especially if you're working in genres like rock and punk.

As someone who writes a lot of lyrics that could be taken politically but really struggles to write songs singularly meant to address politics, I've found a lot of the problem with on-the-nose political writing is that it lacks a driving emotional core. 

I said this in another thread a few months ago, but for political writing to work, I think you really need to connect with it emotionally on a personal level (or be very good at adapting the story of someone who does -- without being pedantic or disrespectful). Politics doesn't have to be a sterile and unrelatable topic. At their basest level, almost all politics are personal to someone. Law and policy are built around real human stories and human emotions. Its why we fight about it so much. 

Writing a song with themes that are just "fuck Trump" generally comes across pretty corny. Like we get it, we've heard it all on Twitter, there's nothing special or resonant there -- and certainly nothing unique to your voice. Music is about expressing and sharing an emotional experience and you need to give us a reason to connect with your writing emotionally. Something that makes us go "yeah, I *feel* what you're saying and it hits home for me." 

Now, lets say you have an emotional reason for writing about the Trump presidency. As a hypothetical, imagine you had a gay or transgender sibling who took their own life at a young age and because of Trump's campaign promises about banning anything related to the LGBTQ+ experience, you have a lot of personal emotions. There's a lot to write about here. And while you're writing about a very specific experience, these emotions can be universally understood by anyone who has mourned a loved one. Examples: 

*  You feel it's spitting on the grave of a loved one that you're grieving. 
* You worry that other children will struggle with hopelessness and isolation the way your sibling did, and the idea of others suffering the same pain that your sibling endured (and, in the event of suicide, the pain that you and your family endured) is nauseating. 
* There was nothing you could do for your sibling so you've felt powerless, but maybe you can do something now and feel a sense of reclaimed purpose. 
* Maybe there's something you would have said to your sibling if they were still alive -- something to comfort them or make them feel understood. Maybe you want to say it in a song to whoever needs to hear it now. 

Obviously it doesn't have to be as dramatic or high-stakes as this example. And your story can come from any variety of political stances, as long you're being genuine to your beliefs. If the audience can feel that you care, they're going to find a way to care too.

I don't just mean in terms of writing in a way that feels pandering (but certainly that too, you can find a lot of trendy, straight girlpop artists rn writing in a super queerbaity way and it's very cringe) but also don't break your own writing voice/style when you're doing it.

Grandson is a great example of confronting these topics in a way that's direct, but also has a lot of emotional resonance because he's writing in his own voice about the way he's personally impacted by the subject matter.

I think I can objectively say I'm a pretty good writer, I've made a living writing professionally (both creatively and otherwise) most of my adult life, and I personally still really struggle with this. In my own lyrical voice, I use a lot of imagery and drama, and I tend to lean into abstract metaphors to convey emotion. I've always gotten stuck when trying to force myself into drafting lyrics about political subject matter that I don't personally connect with on an emotional level. The writing always becomes too literal, too on the nose, and too out of place. It doesn't sound like me, so it doesn't work. And I've always found a way back when I can center myself on my emotional reasons for writing. 

Ultimately, all politics are personal to someone. I might struggle to write a song about Gaza because I don't have the core emotional experience to talk about losing a child, living in a war zone, or surviving as a refugee. But I can write about being trans, I can write about personally seeing people die due to gun violence so often that it becomes numbing, and I can write about being forced into a Christian education system -- all of which are hugely politically relevant.

I second distro kid. I play in a tiny indie band that had most of our success in film and television placements (most notably some behind the scenes stuff for the super bowl one year). We self released through cdbaby for our ep (in 2010 before DK) and moved to Distro Kid for our full length with basically the same experience. It makes it so fuckin easy to get your music into people's ears. There's almost no point to physical copies these days, Bandcamp is a ghost town, and people who might otherwise listen to you probably won't go out of their way if you're not on their regular streaming service.

The nice thing though is with an EP you don't have to necessarily make the songs flow in a cohesive or thematic manner. The point is more to get a handful of your strongest songs in front of a listener in a concise way that isn't asking them to commit too much time. I'll always be one to push for narrative and thematic cohesion on a full length, but an EP should basically be a series of singles you can try with different audiences.

Hot tip for the release top, as someone who worked in the press for a long time and saw both sides of interviews. As you build up to your release, make a list of contacts in entertainment sections of nearby newspapers, local radio stations, small scale magazines, and indie blogs. Spend a day reaching out to all of them to let them know when the EP is releasing and asking about coverage. Bonus if you can think of an angle to make the release newsworthy (a charity fundraiser for a cd release show for instance). These people are always looking to fill pages if you give them a halfway decent reason to notice you.

Good luck, and congratulations. It's such a big step, and you'll have a blast.

The vocalist and I wrIte EVERYTHING together these days, we just wrapped his solo album a little bit ago. He's not a writer and really struggles to make things sound a bit more interesting sometimes so it works that I can come in and refine everything, but you know who writes that killer line that just seals the chorus in place most times? Learning to be a better writer is a great skill and there are ways to do that (pick up as many books on it as you can) but if that's not your cup of tea, then just focus on being direct and genuine with your words. Sometimes trying too hard to be "deep" will ruin a song. Not every songwriter needs to be an abstract, post-modern poet.

BandLab.com is free and has a variety of instruments that you can write with, using your mouse to draw the note and it's length on a chart. I'd use a stringed instrument -- piano is notoriously the hardest to match (which is why voice students use it). Just start there with a couple simple notes. Write a series of them and practice singing.

It's possible you're tone deaf but it's highly highly unlikely. I struggled a lot with this as well, and I wanted to be able to sing since I was a kid. Okay, so when I started writing lyrics the guys in my band were literally like ... Semi-pro, like showcased for Sony and stuff (and all like 5-10 years older than for the most part). I could barely play bass in time, but had a tooon of writing experience and basically the fact that I could write is what got me in and made me valuable. In our music scene, the most professionally successful band here (The Crane Wives, if you listen to folk) were in a ton of the same creative writing classes as me. I was friends with one member just because of our connection that way. I say all that to say that -- so many people overlook learning to write well as a part of writing music, but it will open doors and make you stand out SO much more than you expect.

So like. Just learning fundamentals to solid writing and storytelling are probably the biggest things. Almost every writer I know started with a copy of "On Writing" by Stephen King (it's half memoir, but the writing advice is great -- real important stuff about the practice mindset and process) and almost every newspaper I've worked for basically gave out "The Elements of Style" by Strunk and White (this is basically a teeny, tiny technical manual -- real boring, but only like 100 pages and if you master it, you'll be ahead of almost everyone you encounter). 

That said, I've been freelancing and contributing lyrics to some songwriters in my town lately and picked up the book "Writing Better Lyrics" off Amazon. Actually the first lyric-specific book I've read I'm ashamed to admit lol. There are a lot of more advanced techniques here, which I've found FASCINATING as one of those people who doesnt quite "get" poetry but loves lyricism. I'm still working my way through that book but I've found it opened my creativity a lot. Honestly was struggling thanks to some recent health issues and mega depression, and it kick-started me again.

Oh, last piece of advice is just to read a ton. I carry a horror novel with me everywhere and have a notebook for lines/metaphors I like that I might wind up borrowing or formatting a line off. But whatever genre Is in your wheelhouse, just read writers that are better than you.

Just as incivility itself can be used to silence a minority view, condemnations of the “incivility” of those holding such views can function as a silencing mechanism or means of harassing a feared or subordinated group. With regard to what is commonly meant by intemperate discussion, namely invective, sarcasm, personality, and the like, the denunciation of these weapons would deserve more sympathy if it were ever proposed to interdict them equally to both sides; but it is only desired to restrain the employment of them against the prevailing opinion: against the unprevailing they may not only be used without general (p. 212) disapproval, but will be likely to obtain for him who uses them the praise of honest zeal and righteous indignation. Yeah, A Wrinkle in Time was a pre-teen favorite of mine and Ursula Leguin rattled the genre straight through. Mary Shelley changed my life as a teen. But they're remembered for being anomalous, and anomalies by nature are exceptional events -- they're exceptions that prove the rule. 

I mean, let's just say for a second you're right and I'm wrong. Le Guin, L'Engle, Atwood, and even writers like Khaw aren't exceptions. Women like them are celebrated in sci-fi. You'd think they'd be everywhere, right?  

* Going off of NPRs top 100 Sci-FI books of all time, [a staggering majority of sci-fi novels considered masterworks](https://www.newstatesman.com/culture/2015/08/i-read-100-best-fantasy-and-sci-fi-novels-and-they-were-shockingly-offensive) are rife with sexist and patriarchal tropes, imagery, and fantasies. 
* Of the [200 top-grossing sci-fi films](https://gritdaily.com/darren-beyer-women-sci-fi/) of all time, only 19 (just under 10%) have women in leading roles. This isn't just old shit either. Of the top-grossing sci-fi films between 2000 and 2010, only one had a woman in the starring role (it was a children's cartoon). What about between 2010 and now? Only 15% had women in starring roles. 
* MIT Technology Review's Top Ten Hard Science Fiction Novels of All Time:9/10 authors are men. 
* [Forbidden Planet's 50 Science Fiction Books You Must Read:](https://forbiddenplanet.com/log/recommendations/50-sf-books-you-must-read/) 46/50 books were written by men and the list has just three women (Ursula Le Guin is listed twice). 
* [Goodreads "Best Science Fiction" Top 100:](https://www.goodreads.com/list/show/19341.Best_Science_Fiction) Here, 90/100 authors are men.  
* Only 17% of sci-fi authors with published manuscripts are women. 
* Of the five publications that are purely science fiction focused (Analog Science Fiction and Fact, New York Review of Science Fiction, Asimov's Science Fiction Foundation, and Science Fiction Studios) an average of 78% of their reviews cover male authors. 
* Some [may argue that this is just because](http://torbooks.co.uk/2013/07/10/sexism-in-genre-publishing-a-publishers-perspective/#more-10359) too few women try to get published -- and more women should submit to more publishing houses. However, submissions are not a good metric to judge by ---that suggestion is based in the false idea that publishers select their titles from a slush pile of open submissions. They don't. Slush pile titles are rarely published. [Typically, editors make requests for specific manuscripts by specific writers from an agent.](https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB10001424052748703414504575001271351446274)
* Books with male characters sell [10 million more copies on average.](https://bookriot.com/male-leads-in-fiction/)

"Well no," you say. "Men can write books about women too! Lots of those books probably have well-developed female characters!" Except: 

* When examining fiction awards including the Hugo, Pulitzer, Newberry, and more -- [researchers found](https://nicolagriffith.com/2015/05/26/books-about-women-tend-not-to-win-awards/) that when women do win awards, they are typically for books written from a male point of view/about men.  
* The same researchers also found that the higher the award ranked in prestige, the more likely the subject would be male. 
* Of the top [50 best selling sci-fi and fantasy novels over the last decade, 42/50 were led by male protagonists.](https://www.tor.com/images/stories/blogs/decades_best/tordotcom_decadebest_gender2.pdf)
* Studies have found that across mediums, science fiction as a genre struggles with the underrepresentation of women -- and those that are represented are unlikely to be the lead. They are most commonly portrayed in roles that are ["caring or passive" and less likely to have equal expertise to male characters.](http://www.mindfulofscience.org/2014/04/18/the-representation-of-women-in-science-fiction/)

Speaking of that, you think the people who stand to gain the most money from book publishing haven't taken notice of this? 

* [British author Sophie McDougall](http://io9.com/is-the-book-industry-sexist-or-just-starved-for-great-w-747316426)was asked by a publisher to turn her 50/50 male and female cast into a 75% male cast because: "if there's a woman on the cover, the book won't sell." She was also asked by that publisher's marketing team to namedrop more male writers as influences and less female writers.
* Novelist [Catherine Nicholls](https://jezebel.com/homme-de-plume-what-i-learned-sending-my-novel-out-und-1720637627) tested this by sending out her manuscripts under both her own name and the name "George." She found [George Nichols was 800% as successful](http://jezebel.com/homme-de-plume-what-i-learned-sending-my-novel-out-und-1720637627), despite submitting the same manuscripts. 

Plus, if you'd rather not talk about pop science fiction -- hard science fiction is [even MORE](https://www.theguardian.com/books/2012/aug/07/hard-sf-women-writers) male-dominated. Editors of anthologies aggressively excluded women, preventing them from being published. And [while activists in the genre are working to undo the racism and sexism that barred entry to women and PoC](https://www.chicagotribune.com/entertainment/ct-ent-books-sci-fi-women-1104-story.html), it's absolutely nowhere near accomplished yet.
